nodes.name: Write a linear equation with one, no, or infinitely many solutions
nodes.statement: Write a linear equation in one variable with a required number of solutions by choosing the coefficients of x and the constants on the two sides: different coefficients for one solution, equal coefficients with different constants for no solution, equal coefficients and equal constants for infinitely many.
nodes.assess: Fill in the blanks in 5x - 2 = __x + __ so the equation has no solution. Then fill them in again so it has infinitely many solutions.
procedure: Write each side in the form px + q.
For one solution, give the two sides different coefficients of x.
For no solution, give them the same coefficient of x and different constants.
For infinitely many solutions, give them the same coefficient of x and the same constant.

proposed_edges.rationale: The required outcomes, one solution, no solution, or infinitely many solutions, are the three cases this node asks the learner to produce.
The coefficient and constant rules that decide one, no, or infinitely many solutions are the rules used to choose the blanks.

nodes.name: The graph of an equation in two variables is the set of its solutions
nodes.statement: The graph of an equation in x and y is the set of all points (a, b) such that substituting x = a and y = b makes the equation true.
nodes.assess: Is the point (1, 1) on the graph of 3x + 2y = 5? Is the point (2, 0)?

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement treats each point as a pair (a, b) whose first and second numbers are its two coordinates in the plane.
Deciding whether (1, 1) and (2, 0) lie on 3x + 2y = 5 requires substituting both coordinates and checking the equation.
The statement calls a point part of the graph when its coordinates make the equation true, which is what being a solution means.
Substituting x = a and y = b into the equation to see whether it is true is an evaluation of both sides at given values.

nodes.name: A solution of a system of two equations
nodes.statement: A solution of a system of two equations in x and y is a pair (a, b) that makes both equations true at the same time.
nodes.assess: Is (2, 3) a solution of the system x + y = 5 and 2x - y = 1? Is (1, 4)?

proposed_edges.rationale: The solution is written as an ordered pair (a, b) with the x-value first and the y-value second.
Testing (2, 3) and (1, 4) in x + y = 5 and 2x - y = 1 means substituting into both equations.
A solution of a system is a pair that makes each equation true, so what it means to satisfy one equation is used twice.
Deciding whether (2, 3) or (1, 4) is a solution means substituting the pair into both equations and evaluating each side.

nodes.name: Solutions of a system as the intersection points of the graphs
nodes.statement: The solutions of a system of two linear equations in two variables are exactly the points where their graphs intersect, because a point lies on both graphs exactly when its coordinates satisfy both equations.
nodes.assess: Point P lies on the graph of the first equation of a system but not on the graph of the second. Point Q is where the two graphs cross. Which point's coordinates solve the system, and why do the other point's coordinates not?

proposed_edges.rationale: The because-clause says a point is on a graph exactly when its coordinates satisfy the equation, which is the graph-as-solution-set idea.
The statement identifies the intersection points with the pairs that make both equations true, which is the meaning of a solution of the system.

nodes.name: Read the solution of a system from its drawn graphs
nodes.statement: When the graphs of the two equations of a system are drawn, the solution is the coordinate pair of the point where the lines cross.
nodes.assess: The graphs of the two equations of a system are drawn on a coordinate grid and cross at a grid point (shown). What is the solution of the system?
procedure: Find the point where the two lines cross.
Read its coordinates (x, y); that pair is the solution.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 2 reads the x and y coordinates of the crossing point, which may lie in any quadrant of the grid.
The procedure answers with the solution of the system, so the learner must know a solution is the pair satisfying both equations.

nodes.name: Estimate the solution of a system by graphing
nodes.statement: Estimate the solution of a system of two equations of the form y = mx + b by graphing both lines on the same axes and reading the coordinates of their intersection, estimating them when the intersection is not at a grid point.
nodes.assess: Graph y = x + 1 and y = -2x + 6 on the same axes and estimate the solution of the system.
procedure: Graph each equation as a line on the same coordinate axes.
Locate the point where the lines cross.
Read or estimate its coordinates.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 3 estimates coordinates when the crossing falls between grid points, as the lines in the test problem cross at fractional coordinates.
Step 1 graphs each equation y = mx + b as a line, by plotting two points and drawing the line through them.
Steps 2 and 3 find the crossing point and take its coordinates as the solution, which is reading a solution from drawn graphs.

nodes.name: Tell by inspection how many solutions a simple system has
nodes.statement: For a system written as ax + by = c and dx + ey = f: if the left side of one equation is k times the left side of the other, the system has infinitely many solutions when the right sides are in the same ratio k and no solution when they are not; otherwise it has exactly one solution.
nodes.assess: Without solving, say how many solutions each system has: 3x + 2y = 5 and 3x + 2y = 6; x + y = 4 and 2x + 2y = 8; x + y = 4 and x - y = 2.
procedure: Write both equations with the x and y terms on the left and the constant on the right.
Check whether the left side of one equation is a number k times the left side of the other.
If not, the system has exactly one solution. If so, compare the right sides: k times the other right side means infinitely many solutions, anything else means no solution.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 1 moves the x and y terms to the left and the constant to the right by doing the same operation to both sides.
The conclusions are counts of solutions of a system, one, none or infinitely many, so what a solution of a system is must be known.
Step 2 finds the number k that multiplies one left side into the other by dividing coefficients, which may be fractions or negative.
Step 2 checks whether one left side is a number k times the other, which multiplies the coefficients by k and compares.

nodes.name: The number of solutions of a system from the slopes and intercepts of its lines
nodes.statement: For a system of two equations of the form y = mx + b, different slopes give lines that cross once (one solution); equal slopes with different intercepts give parallel lines (no solution); equal slopes with equal intercepts give the same line (infinitely many solutions).
nodes.assess: Without graphing or solving, say how many solutions each system has: y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x - 3; y = 2x + 1 and y = -x + 1; y = 2x + 1 and y = 1 + 2x.

proposed_edges.rationale: Seeing that y = 1 + 2x is the same equation as y = 2x + 1 in the test problem needs reordering the terms of a sum.
The statement is written for equations y = mx + b, where m is the slope and b is the y-intercept of the line.
The statement turns crossing, parallel and coinciding lines into one, none or infinitely many solutions, which is the solutions-as-intersection fact.
Equal slopes with different intercepts give parallel lines, and the statement uses that parallel lines never meet to conclude no solution.

nodes.name: Solve a system of two equations y = mx + b by setting the expressions equal
nodes.statement: When both equations of a system give y in terms of x, solve the system by setting the two expressions for y equal, solving that equation for x, and substituting to find y.
nodes.assess: Solve the system y = 3x - 2 and y = x + 4.
procedure: Set the two expressions for y equal to each other.
Solve the resulting equation for x.
Substitute that value of x into either equation to find y.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 2 solves the equation formed by the two expressions, which has x on both sides, as in 3x - 2 = x + 4.
Step 3 substitutes the value found for x into an expression for y and evaluates it to get y.
Setting the two expressions for y equal rests on a solution being one pair whose y-value satisfies both equations at once.

nodes.name: Solve a system of two linear equations by substitution
nodes.statement: Solve a system of two linear equations by expressing one variable in terms of the other from one equation, substituting that expression into the other equation, solving for the remaining variable, and substituting back.
nodes.assess: Solve the system y = 2x + 1 and 3x + y = 11 by substitution.
procedure: If neither equation is already solved for a variable, solve one of them for one variable.
Substitute that expression for the variable in the other equation.
Solve the resulting one-variable equation.
Substitute the value back to find the other variable.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 1 solves one equation for one variable, which is done by applying the same operation to both sides of that equation.
Step 3 solves the one-variable equation that results, which needs combining like terms and sometimes expanding, as in 3x + (2x + 1) = 11.
Step 3 solves the resulting one-variable linear equation, which may need expanding and collecting terms.
Step 2 replaces a variable by a whole expression, which must be treated as one quantity, in parentheses, inside the other equation.
Step 4 substitutes the value of the first variable back into an expression for the other variable and evaluates it.
The method finds the pair that satisfies both equations, so the meaning of a solution of a system is used throughout.

nodes.name: Solve a system of two linear equations by elimination
nodes.statement: Solve a system of two linear equations by adding or subtracting the equations, after multiplying one or both by a number if needed, so that one variable is eliminated; then solve for the other variable and substitute back.
nodes.assess: Solve the system 2x + 3y = 12 and 2x - y = 4 by elimination.
procedure: Multiply one or both equations by numbers so that one variable has equal or opposite coefficients.
Subtract the equations if the coefficients are equal, or add them if they are opposite, to eliminate that variable.
Solve the resulting one-variable equation.
Substitute the value back to find the other variable.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 1 multiplies both sides of an equation by a number, an operation that keeps the solutions of the equation.
Step 3 solves an equation like 4y = 8 that remains once one variable has been eliminated.
Step 4 substitutes into an original equation and solves the result, of the form px + q = r, for the other variable.
Step 3 solves the one-variable equation left after elimination, whose coefficient may be negative or a fraction.
Step 2 adds the two equations, so the left sides are added as linear expressions and like terms are combined.
Multiplying an equation by a number multiplies every term of its left side, as in 3(2x - y) = 6x - 3y.
Step 2 also subtracts one equation from the other, so one left side is subtracted from the other as linear expressions.
Step 4 substitutes the value found back into an equation to find the other variable.
The method finds the pair that satisfies both equations, so the meaning of a solution of a system is used throughout.

nodes.name: Find where two lines meet when each is given by its y-intercept and a slope or second point, with an integer meeting point
nodes.statement: Solve mathematical problems about two lines, each given by its y-intercept together with its slope or one other point, that meet at a point with integer coordinates, by writing both equations as y = mx + b and solving the system.
nodes.assess: Line A passes through (0, 1) and (2, 5). Line B passes through (0, 7) and (3, 4). At what point do the two lines meet?

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement writes each line as y = mx + b from its y-intercept and slope.
With both lines written as y = mx + b, the meeting point is found by setting the two expressions for y equal and solving.
Where the two lines meet is the solution of the system of their equations, which turns the geometric question into solving a system.
When a line is given by its y-intercept and a second point, the slope is found from those two points.

nodes.name: Decide whether and where two lines given by two points each intersect
nodes.statement: For two lines, each given by any two of its points, decide whether they intersect and, if they do, find the intersection point, which may have fraction coordinates, by writing an equation for each line and solving the system.
nodes.assess: Does the line through (1, 2) and (3, 6) meet the line through (0, 5) and (5, 0)? If so, at what point?

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement writes an equation for each line, in the form y = mx + b once m and b are known.
A line given by two points may pass through the origin, as in the assessment, and then its equation is y = mx.
When neither given point is on the y-axis, b must be found from the two points before y = mx + b can be written.
Finding the intersection, possibly with fraction coordinates, sets the two expressions for y equal and solves for x.
Deciding whether the lines intersect uses that equal slopes with different intercepts give parallel lines with no common point.
The intersection point of the two lines is the solution of the system of their equations, which is what the problem asks for.
A line given by any two of its points has its slope found from those two points before an equation can be written.

nodes.name: Solve real-world problems about when two constant-rate quantities are equal
nodes.statement: Solve real-world problems about two quantities that each start at a given value and change at a constant rate, finding when they are equal, by writing two equations of the form y = mx + b and solving the system, in problems whose answers are whole numbers.
nodes.assess: Plan A costs $20 plus $5 per month. Plan B costs $50 plus $2 per month. After how many months do the two plans cost the same, and what is that cost?

proposed_edges.rationale: Each quantity with a starting value and constant rate is written as y = mx + b, which constructs its linear function.
When the two quantities are equal, their expressions of the form y = mx + b are set equal and solved for x.
The time at which the quantities are equal is the pair satisfying both equations at once, a solution of the system.

nodes.name: Solve real-world problems about two unknowns given two linear conditions
nodes.statement: Solve real-world problems about two unknown quantities related by two linear conditions, such as a total count and a total value, by writing a system of two linear equations and solving it algebraically.
nodes.assess: A club sold 20 tickets, some at $2 and some at $5, and took in $76. How many tickets of each price did it sell?

proposed_edges.rationale: Each condition is written with letters for the two unknown counts, such as 2x + 5y for the total value of the tickets.
The system of two linear equations is solved algebraically by adding or subtracting the equations to eliminate one variable.
The two conditions become two equations that the unknown pair must satisfy together, which is a solution of a system.
The system is solved algebraically, for example by solving x + y = 20 for y and substituting into the value equation.

nodes.name: A function assigns to each input exactly one output
nodes.statement: A function is a rule that assigns to each input exactly one output.
nodes.assess: Rule A takes a positive whole number and gives any whole number smaller than it. Rule B takes a positive whole number and gives the number 1 less than it. Which rule is a function?

nodes.name: Decide from a table of pairs whether a relationship is a function
nodes.statement: A table or list of input-output pairs fits a function exactly when no input is paired with two different outputs; the same output may appear for different inputs.
nodes.assess: Does each table show y as a function of x? Table 1: (1, 3), (2, 5), (1, 4). Table 2: (1, 3), (2, 3), (3, 3).
procedure: Look for any input that appears more than once.
If a repeated input has two different outputs, the relationship is not a function; otherwise the listed pairs fit a function.

proposed_edges.rationale: Table 1 in the test problem is given as a list of ordered pairs, each written (input, output).
Step 1 scans the input column of a table for repeated inputs and reads the output paired with each.
A table fits a function exactly when each input has one output, which restates the definition of a function for pairs.

nodes.name: The graph of a function is the set of its input-output pairs
nodes.statement: The graph of a function is the set of all points (x, y) in the coordinate plane where x is an input and y is the output the function assigns to x.
nodes.assess: The point (3, 7) is on the graph of a function. What output does the function give for the input 3? Must the point (7, 3) also be on the graph?

proposed_edges.rationale: The point (x, y) has first coordinate x and second coordinate y, which is why (7, 3) differs from (3, 7).
Each point of the graph pairs an input with the single output the function assigns to it, as the definition says.

nodes.name: Decide from a graph whether y is a function of x
nodes.statement: A graph in the coordinate plane shows y as a function of x exactly when no vertical line meets it in more than one point, since two points on one vertical line are one input with two outputs.
nodes.assess: Which of these graphs show y as a function of x: a circle; a V shape opening upward; a vertical line; a horizontal line?
procedure: Picture vertical lines placed across the whole graph.
If some vertical line meets the graph in two or more points, y is not a function of x; otherwise it is.

proposed_edges.rationale: The criterion holds because a function gives each input exactly one output, so a repeated input with two outputs fails.
The test reads points of the graph as input-output pairs, so two points on one vertical line are two outputs of one input.

nodes.name: Compare the rates of change of two linear functions given in different forms
nodes.statement: Given two linear functions represented in different ways (equation, table, graph, or verbal description), find the rate of change of each and decide which is greater.
nodes.assess: Function A is y = 3x + 2. Function B is given by the table x: 0, 2, 4 and y: 1, 9, 17. Which function has the greater rate of change?
procedure: Find each function's rate of change from its representation: m in y = mx + b, or the change in y divided by the change in x between two points of a table or graph.
Compare the two rates.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement compares two functions, each assigning one output to every input.
A linear function is given by an equation y = mx + b, one of the representations the node compares.
Step 1 takes the rate of change to be m in y = mx + b, so the meaning of m in that form is used.
A function given by a verbal description has its rate of change read from the words, as step 1 allows.
Step 1 finds the rate as the change in y over the change in x between two points of a table or a graph.
Step 2 decides which rate is greater, and rates can be negative fractions or decimals.

nodes.name: Compare the initial values of two linear functions given in different forms
nodes.statement: Given two linear functions represented in different ways (equation, table, graph, or verbal description), find the initial value of each, the output for input 0, and decide which is greater.
nodes.assess: Function A is y = 4x + 1. Function B is given by the table x: 1, 2, 3 and y: 5, 7, 9. Which function has the greater initial value?
procedure: Find each function's initial value: b in y = mx + b, the y-intercept of a graph, or, for a table, the output reached by working back to input 0 at the constant rate.
Compare the two initial values.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement compares two functions, each assigning one output to every input, at input 0.
A linear function is given by an equation y = mx + b, one of the representations the node compares.
Step 1 takes the initial value to be b in y = mx + b, so the meaning of b in that form is used.
A function given by a verbal description has its initial value read from the words, as step 1 allows.
Step 1 finds the initial value from a table or graph, working back to input 0 at the constant rate.
Step 2 decides which initial value is greater, and initial values can be negative fractions or decimals.

nodes.name: An equation y = mx + b defines a linear function
nodes.statement: Every equation that can be written in the form y = mx + b, for numbers m and b, defines y as a linear function of x.
nodes.assess: Which of these define y as a linear function of x: y = 3x - 2; y = x^2 + 1; y = 5; y = 2/x; y = 7 - x/2?

proposed_edges.rationale: The form y = mx + b writes the product of m and x by placing them side by side.
Recognizing y = 7 - x/2 as the form mx + b requires reordering its terms into x-term then constant.
The form y = mx + b uses letters for the input, the output, and the numbers m and b.
The claim is that the equation defines y as a function of x, which means each x gives exactly one y.

nodes.name: The graphs of linear functions are the non-vertical straight lines
nodes.statement: The graph of a linear function is a straight line that is not vertical, and every straight line in the coordinate plane that is not vertical is the graph of a linear function.
nodes.assess: Which of these are graphs of linear functions: a slanted straight line; a horizontal straight line; a vertical straight line; a curve through (0, 0), (1, 1) and (2, 4)?

proposed_edges.rationale: The graph of a function is the set of its input-output points, which is the object the statement says is a line.
Vertical lines are excluded because two points on a vertical line give one input two outputs, so they are not graphs of functions.
The statement says the graph is a straight line, so what a straight line is must be known.
The statement is about the graphs of functions defined by y = mx + b, so what a linear function is must be known.
The converse claim says every non-vertical line has an equation y = mx + b, which is writing such an equation for a line.
Non-vertical lines through the origin have equations y = mx, which the converse claim also covers.

nodes.name: Graph a linear function from its equation y = mx + b
nodes.statement: Graph y = mx + b by plotting two points whose coordinates satisfy the equation and drawing the straight line through them.
nodes.assess: Graph y = -2x + 3.
procedure: Plot the point (0, b).
Substitute another value of x into the equation to find a second point, and plot it.
Draw the straight line through the two points.

proposed_edges.rationale: Steps 1 and 2 plot the points (0, b) and a second point, whose coordinates may be negative.
The procedure plots points whose coordinates satisfy the equation, because the graph is the set of such points.
Step 2 substitutes another value of x into mx + b and evaluates to find the second point's y.
Step 3 draws the straight line through the two points, extended in both directions.
Drawing the straight line through two plotted points is valid because the graph of y = mx + b is a straight line.
Evaluating mx + b adds a signed constant to the product.
Evaluating mx at a chosen x multiplies signed numbers, since m may be negative or a fraction.

nodes.name: Show from its values that a function is not linear
nodes.statement: A function is not linear if the rate of change, the change in output divided by the change in input, differs between two pairs of its points; if the rate is the same for every pair of listed points, those points lie on one line.
nodes.assess: The area of a square is A = s^2. Use the side lengths s = 1, 2 and 3 to decide whether A is a linear function of s.
procedure: Take pairs of points from the table or rule.
Compute the rate of change for each pair.
If two rates differ, the function is not linear.

proposed_edges.rationale: The test problem evaluates A = s^2 at s = 1, 2 and 3, which needs squares of whole numbers.
Step 1 takes pairs of points from a rule by evaluating the rule at chosen inputs.
The statement says points of a linear function lie on one line, which is the meaning of a linear function.
Step 2 computes the change in output over the change in input for each pair of points.
Differing rates between pairs show a function is not linear because the rate between any two points of a line is the same.

nodes.name: Give an example of a function that is not linear
nodes.statement: Produce a function that is not linear and show that it is not linear by exhibiting three of its points that do not lie on one line.
nodes.assess: Give a rule for a function that is not linear, and use three of its points to show that it is not linear.
procedure: Choose a rule whose output does not change by equal amounts for equal changes in input, such as squaring the input.
Compute three points of the rule.
Show that the rates of change between two pairs of these points differ, so the points are not on one line.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 2 computes three points of the chosen rule by evaluating it at three inputs.
The example must be a function, a rule giving each input exactly one output, before it can be shown not linear.
Step 3 shows two rates differ between pairs of the three points, which is the test for a function not being linear.

nodes.name: Describe where a graphed relationship is increasing, decreasing, or constant
nodes.statement: From a graph relating two quantities, describe the intervals of the input over which the output increases, decreases, or stays the same as the input increases.
nodes.assess: The graph shown gives the height of a hot-air balloon over 60 minutes. Describe in words when the height increases, stays the same, and decreases.

proposed_edges.rationale: The graph relates two quantities, so each point must be read as a pair of values in the situation, such as a time and a height.
Describing a graph means reading output values at inputs along the horizontal axis and seeing how they change.
Output and input are the dependent and independent quantities, with the input on the horizontal axis.

nodes.name: Tell from a graph where a relationship changes at a constant or a changing rate
nodes.statement: From a graph relating two quantities, tell the intervals where the relationship is linear (the graph is straight, so the output changes at a constant rate) and where it is nonlinear (the graph curves, so the rate changes).
nodes.assess: The graph shown gives the distance a car has traveled over 10 minutes. Over which interval does the car travel at a constant speed, and over which is its speed changing?

proposed_edges.rationale: The graph relates two quantities, so each point must be read as a pair of values in the situation, such as a time and a distance.
Telling straight parts from curved parts means reading how output values change along the horizontal axis of a graph.
A constant rate of change, such as constant speed, is a rate described in per language, and the statement tells constant from changing rate.

nodes.name: Sketch a graph from a verbal description of a relationship
nodes.statement: Sketch a graph, without a numerical scale, whose increasing, decreasing, constant, straight and curved parts match a verbal description of how one quantity changes with another.
nodes.assess: Sketch a graph of the temperature of a cup of hot cocoa over one hour: it cools quickly at first, then more slowly, and then stays at room temperature.

proposed_edges.rationale: Drawing the graph puts the two quantities of the situation on labeled axes, as in graphing paired quantities.
The sketch is drawn on labeled axes meeting at an origin, without a numerical scale.
The sketch must show increasing, decreasing and constant parts that match the description, so those parts of a graph must be known.
The sketch must show straight and curved parts that match constant and changing rates in the description.
Deciding which quantity goes on the horizontal axis and which on the vertical axis follows from independent and dependent.

nodes.name: Add multi-digit whole numbers
nodes.statement: Find the sum of multi-digit whole numbers, with sums up to 1,000,000, accurately and without objects, by any reliable method; place-value strategies and the standard algorithm both meet it.
nodes.assess: Find 4,827 + 3,596 and 26,054 + 8,968. Use any method.

proposed_edges.rationale: Adding numbers with more digits uses the same sum-finding on each place, extending the sums found within 1000.
Sums up to 1,000,000 compose a unit of the next place from ten in any place, thousands and ten-thousands included.

nodes.name: Divide by a two-digit number, no remainder
nodes.statement: Find the whole-number quotient of a dividend of up to four digits by a two-digit divisor that divides it exactly, by any reliable method; partial quotients, an area model with numbers, and the standard algorithm all meet it.
nodes.assess: Find 7,452 divided by 36 and 96 divided by 12. Use any method.

proposed_edges.rationale: Finding a quotient of a dividend up to four digits is the same task with a larger divisor, using the same place-by-place reasoning.
Any method forms multiples of the two-digit divisor, such as 36 x 7, and compares them with the dividend.
Each method subtracts multiples of the divisor from a dividend of up to four digits, which exceeds subtracting within 1000.
Quotients of up to three digits need multiples of the divisor times tens and hundreds, found by place value.

nodes.name: Divide by a two-digit number with a remainder
nodes.statement: Find the whole-number quotient and the remainder of a dividend of up to four digits by a two-digit divisor, with the remainder less than the divisor, by any reliable method.
nodes.assess: Find the quotient and remainder of 200 divided by 60, and of 1,000 divided by 24. Use any method.

proposed_edges.rationale: The quotient is found as in division by a two-digit number with no remainder, then a remainder is left over.
The statement requires the remainder to be less than the divisor, which is what the remainder means.

nodes.name: A remainder is what is left after making as many whole groups as possible
nodes.statement: When a whole number of objects is put into as many groups of a given size as possible, the objects left over are the remainder; the remainder is always less than the group size, since otherwise one more group could be made.
nodes.assess: 17 cubes are put into towers of 5 cubes. How many full towers are made, and how many cubes are left over? Could 6 cubes be left over? Why or why not?

proposed_edges.rationale: The reason a remainder is less than the group size compares two numbers: a leftover as large as the group size would make another group.
The remainder is what is left after putting objects into as many equal groups of a given size as possible.

nodes.name: Dividing by a and then by b is dividing by a x b
nodes.statement: For nonzero whole numbers a and b, dividing a number by a and then dividing the result by b gives the same quotient as dividing the number by a x b.
nodes.assess: Maya divides 720 by 8 and then divides that answer by 10. Without computing, what single division gives the same answer?

proposed_edges.rationale: The rule is about dividing a number by a, then dividing the result by b, so the meaning of a quotient is used.
Dividing by a then by b is read as two unknown-factor equations, n = a x m and m = b x q.
Combining the two equations gives n = a x (b x q) = (a x b) x q, which needs the associative property.
The test problem needs the single divisor 8 x 10 = 80 to name the equivalent division.

nodes.name: Judge whether the answer to a multistep word problem is reasonable by estimating
nodes.statement: An answer to a multistep whole-number word problem with multi-digit numbers and the four operations is judged reasonable or not by estimating the answer with rounded numbers or mental computation and comparing.
nodes.assess: Lee says 4 boxes of 198 nails, minus 305 nails used, leaves 1,097 nails. Without computing exactly, use rounding to decide whether his answer is reasonable, and explain.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement is about multistep problems with multi-digit numbers, so the operations the story needs must be identified to estimate.
Judging an answer by estimating and comparing is the method of the two-step version, here extended to multi-digit numbers.
The estimate uses rounded numbers, and multi-digit numbers must be rounded to a suitable place such as the nearest hundred.
The estimate is made by rounding the numbers, as in rounding 198 to 200 and 305 to 300.

nodes.name: Subtracting fractions as comparing parts of the same whole
nodes.statement: Subtracting one fraction from another also tells how much more the first amount is than the second: the difference is the part that would have to be joined to the smaller amount to make the larger, where both fractions refer to the same whole.
nodes.assess: Using one bar as the whole, show how much more 5/6 is than 2/6, and say what the difference counts.

proposed_edges.rationale: The difference is described as the part joined to the smaller amount to make the larger, which is joining fractions.
The statement requires both fractions to refer to the same whole for the comparison to make sense.
Saying what the difference between 5/6 and 2/6 counts means seeing 3/6 as three parts of size 1/6 on the bar.
The statement gives a second meaning for subtracting fractions, so the first meaning of separating parts must be known.

nodes.name: The number halfway between two numbers
nodes.statement: The number halfway between two numbers is the point of the number line at the same distance from both: the smaller number plus half of the distance from it to the larger.
nodes.assess: What number is halfway between 40 and 50? Between 200 and 300? Between 4 and 6?

proposed_edges.rationale: The test problem needs half of 10, half of 100 and half of 2, which are divisions by 2.
Half of the distance is the size of each share when the distance is shared into two equal parts.
The halfway number is a point of the number line, which shows whole numbers as lengths from 0.
The distance from the smaller to the larger number on the number line is their difference, and halfway is half of it.

nodes.name: Count by twos from 0 to 20
nodes.statement: Say the multiples of two in order from zero: two, four, six, ..., twenty.
nodes.assess: Count aloud by twos from 0 to 20.

proposed_edges.rationale: The multiples of two are every second number word in the counting sequence, up to twenty.

nodes.name: Count by twenty-fives from 0 to 100
nodes.statement: Say the multiples of twenty-five in order from zero: twenty-five, fifty, seventy-five, one hundred.
nodes.assess: Count aloud by twenty-fives from 0 to 100.

proposed_edges.rationale: The multiples of twenty-five are number words within the sequence up to one hundred, said in order.

nodes.name: The number after nine hundred ninety-nine is one thousand
nodes.statement: The number after nine hundred ninety-nine is one thousand, written 1000; counting by hundreds, one thousand comes after nine hundred.
nodes.assess: What number comes right after 999? Count by hundreds from seven hundred: what comes after nine hundred?

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement names the number after 999 in the counting sequence, so the sequence up to 999 must be known.
Counting by hundreds to nine hundred uses 100, 200, through 900 as numbers of hundreds, and one thousand comes next.

nodes.name: The period names thousand and million
nodes.statement: In the name of a large whole number, the words thousand and million name periods: the number said before thousand counts thousands, and the number said before million counts millions.
nodes.assess: In the number name six million, two hundred thousand, fifteen, which number counts the millions and which counts the thousands?

proposed_edges.rationale: The word thousand names a period, so the number one thousand and its word must already be known.
The number said before thousand or million is a number name below one thousand, such as two hundred or fifteen.

nodes.name: Ordered pair notation
nodes.statement: An ordered pair (a, b) writes two numbers in parentheses, separated by a comma, in a fixed order, first a and then b; (a, b) and (b, a) are different pairs unless a = b.
nodes.assess: Write the ordered pair whose first number is 3 and whose second number is 7. Is (3, 7) the same pair as (7, 3)?

proposed_edges.rationale: The pair is written as two numerals inside parentheses, such as 3 and 7.
The pair has a fixed order, first number then second number, so the ordinal words first and second are used.

nodes.name: Read paired values from a table or a graph
nodes.statement: When pairs of values of two quantities are shown, the value of the second quantity that goes with a given value of the first is read in the same row of a table, or at the point of the graph above that value on the horizontal axis.
nodes.assess: A table shows hours 1, 2, 3, 4 and miles 6, 12, 18, 24. How many miles go with 3 hours? On a graph of the same pairs, what is the y-value of the point above x = 4?

proposed_edges.rationale: Reading the y-value of the point above a given x-value on a graph is reading a coordinate of a point in the first quadrant.
Reading the second value in the same row as a given first value is reading an entry of a table of rows and columns.

nodes.name: The parts of a day in order
nodes.statement: A day goes in order through morning, afternoon, evening and night, and then the next morning begins; events of a day can be placed in that order.
nodes.assess: Which comes first in a day, waking up in the morning or eating lunch in the afternoon? Which part of the day comes after the evening?

nodes.name: An hour is 60 minutes
nodes.statement: In one hour the minute hand goes once around the clock, passing 60 minute marks, so an hour is 60 minutes; the minutes past an hour run from 0 to 59, and at 60 minutes the next hour begins.
nodes.assess: A clock shows 7:59. What time does it show one minute later? How many minutes are in one hour?

proposed_edges.rationale: Counting the 60 minute marks the minute hand passes uses the counting sequence by ones up to sixty.
The statement follows the minute hand once around the clock face, and each hour the minute hand returns to the 12.
The test problem shows the time 7:59 in digital notation, so the hour and minutes of a written time must be read.
